title: Strengthen
summary: Find the new fact that makes the conclusion more likely. Close the gap, or rule out the alternative the argument ignored.

slides.title: Patch the gap
body: Strengthen is weaken in reverse. Find the gap, then look for a fact that makes it smaller.
Two ways to do that: support the assumption directly, or knock out the most obvious alternative explanation. The answer needn’t prove the conclusion; it only has to make it more likely.
slides.callout: Ask: what is the author worried I’ll say? The right answer takes that objection off the table.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
Which one of the following, if true, provides the most support for the conclusion?
Which one of the following, if true, most helps to support the hypothesis?
Each of the following, if true, strengthens the argument EXCEPT:

steps.label: Conclusion and evidence
steps.do: Note what kind of conclusion it is: cause, prediction, plan, comparison.

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.do: What would a skeptic say? Name the alternative the author ignored.

steps.label: Predict
steps.do: A fact that rules out that alternative, or confirms the link between evidence and conclusion.

steps.label: Test each choice
steps.do: Assume it’s true. Does the conclusion become more likely? Pick the one that does the most.

slides.title: Level 1: rule out the other explanation
slides.stimulus: Café owner: Last month I switched to a new brand of coffee beans at my café. Since then, coffee sales have risen by 20 percent compared with the month before. I made no changes to my prices. Clearly, the new beans are what attracted the extra business.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the café owner's argument?

choices.A: Several regular customers have told the owner that they liked the old beans better.
choices.B: The new beans are sold by a roaster that also supplies many other cafés in the city.
choices.C: Sales of the café's tea and pastries did not rise over the same period.
choices.D: Coffee has been the café's best-selling drink for as long as the café has been open.
choices.E: The new beans cost the café less per pound than the old beans did.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: The new beans brought in the extra business.
steps.highlight: the new beans are what attracted the extra business

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Coffee sales rose after the switch.
steps.highlight: coffee sales have risen by 20 percent compared with the month before

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Something else may have brought more customers, such as a busier street. Then every kind of sale would rise, not only coffee.

steps.label: Predict and test
steps.note: The answer should show there was no general rise in customers. C does that: tea and pastries stayed flat. A hurts the argument, and B, D and E do not touch the gap.

why.A: This weakens the argument, so it is the wrong direction.
why.B: On topic, but who sells the beans says nothing about why sales rose.
why.C: Correct. If other sales stayed flat, a general rise in customers is unlikely, so the beans are more likely the cause.
why.D: Past best-seller status does not show why sales rose last month.
why.E: Lower cost affects profit, not what attracted the extra business.

slides.title: Level 2: the method, step by step
slides.stimulus: Archaeologist: Pottery at the Teral site bears glazes made with a mineral found only in mountains 400 kilometers to the north. So the people of Teral must have traded with communities living in those mountains.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the archaeologist's argument?

choices.A: There is no evidence that the people of Teral ever traveled more than a few kilometers from their settlement.
choices.B: Pottery made at Teral has also been found at sites far to the south.
choices.C: Mountain communities used the mineral for purposes other than glazing.
choices.D: Glazes made with the mineral were prized for their color.
choices.E: Some pottery at Teral bears glazes made with local minerals.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.note: Teral traded with the northern mountain communities.
steps.highlight: must have traded with communities living in those mountains

steps.label: Evidence
steps.note: Their glaze uses a mineral found only in those mountains.
steps.highlight: a mineral found only in mountains 400 kilometers to the north

steps.label: Gap
steps.note: The mineral could have reached Teral without trade: Teral people might have gone north and dug it up themselves.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: A strengthener rules that out: evidence they didn’t travel there.

why.A: Correct. If Teral people didn't travel far, they didn't fetch the mineral themselves, which makes trade more likely.
why.B: Trade to the south says nothing about how the mineral arrived from the north.
why.C: Other uses of the mineral don't show how it reached Teral.
why.D: Why the glaze was valued doesn't show it came by trade.
why.E: Local glazes are irrelevant to the imported mineral.

slides.title: Level 3: a selection effect hiding in the comparison
slides.stimulus: Agricultural researcher: Over the past decade, farms in the Calder Valley that switched from sprinklers to drip irrigation have earned, on average, 18 percent more per acre than farms that kept their sprinklers. The researcher surveyed 200 farms chosen at random from county records. Drip systems are costly to install, and most owners have to borrow to pay for them. The gap appeared in every one of the ten years surveyed. These figures show that drip irrigation raises a farm's earnings per acre.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's argument?

choices.A: Drip irrigation systems have been sold in the Calder Valley for about ten years by two competing dealers.
choices.B: Banks in the valley were more willing to lend to farms with a record of high earnings than to farms with a record of low earnings.
choices.C: Agricultural economists who reviewed the researcher's figures found no errors in how earnings per acre were calculated.
choices.D: Many of the valley's farms have been owned by the same families for more than fifty years.
choices.E: Before any farm switched, the farms that later adopted drip irrigation earned about the same per acre as the farms that never did.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: Drip irrigation is what raises earnings per acre.
steps.highlight: drip irrigation raises a farm's earnings per acre

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Switchers earn 18 percent more than farms that kept sprinklers.
steps.highlight: earned, on average, 18 percent more per acre than farms that kept their sprinklers

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Drip is costly and owners must borrow, so the farms that switched may already have been richer or better run.
steps.highlight: most owners have to borrow to pay for them

steps.label: Predict the fix
steps.note: The best strengthener shows the two groups started out equal. No earnings gap before the switch means the switch is a better suspect.

steps.label: Name the traps
steps.note: B backs the selection story, so it weakens. C supports the figures, but the figures already stand. A and D are about the valley, not the gap. The key is a before-the-switch fact, not a fact about irrigation.

why.A: Irrelevant. Who sold the systems and for how long does not address why switchers earn more.
why.B: Weakens. If lenders favored high earners, the adopters may have been the high earners to begin with.
why.C: Supports the premise only. The figures are taken as true, and correct figures still leave the gap open.
why.D: Irrelevant. Family ownership has no link to irrigation or earnings.
why.E: Correct. If the groups earned the same before the switch, the later gap is more likely due to drip irrigation.

slides.title: Level 4: who produced the growth?
slides.stimulus: Between 1820 and 1860, the share of Brindle Island households that kept written account books rose from under a tenth to nearly half. Over the same forty years, the island's wool exports more than tripled. Some islanders credit a new overseas market that opened in 1835, but the price paid for wool was no higher in 1860 than in 1820. Because careful record-keeping shows a household which of its activities earn money, the historian Ilse Varga argues that the spread of account-keeping was a major cause of the growth in wool exports.
slides.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's argument?

choices.A: Wool exports from Brindle Island grew faster between 1820 and 1860 than the wool exports of any neighboring island.
choices.B: Nearly all of the growth in the island's wool exports came from households that began keeping account books after 1820.
choices.C: Nearly all of the growth in the island's wool exports came from households that had kept account books since before 1820.
choices.D: Households that kept account books in 1860 were, on average, wealthier than households that did not.
choices.E: Nearly all of the households on the island that raised sheep in 1860 also grew grain.

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: The spread of account-keeping was a major cause of the wool growth.
steps.highlight: the spread of account-keeping was a major cause of the growth in wool exports

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Two trends ran together. The historian also removes one rival, the market, because prices stayed flat.
steps.highlight: the price paid for wool was no higher in 1860 than in 1820

steps.label: Find the gap
steps.note: Two trends over the same years do not show that the same households are involved. The growth could have come from households the spread never touched.

steps.label: Predict
steps.note: A strengthener ties the growth to households that took up account-keeping during the period.

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: C is B with one idea changed. Growth from households that kept books since before 1820 did not come from the spread, so C weakens. B is the key.

why.A: Out of scope. Comparing with other islands says nothing about account-keeping.
why.B: Correct. It ties the growth to households that adopted account books during the period, closing the gap.
why.C: The near-twin that weakens. Growth from long-time keepers did not come from the spread of the practice.
why.D: Weakens. Wealth is a rival explanation for greater wool output.
why.E: Irrelevant. Growing grain has no link to account-keeping or to wool exports.

traps.name: Restates a premise
traps.tell: Repeats the evidence in new words. It adds nothing.

traps.name: Sounds related
traps.tell: On topic, but doesn’t touch the gap, like other uses of the mineral.

traps.name: The weakener
traps.tell: Does the reverse. Easy to pick on a long question.

traps.name: Supports something else
traps.tell: Makes a nearby claim more likely, not the conclusion itself.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Name the skeptic’s objection; the answer removes it.
Causal claim? Rule out another cause, or show the effect tracks the cause.
